section.title: Sing to the Lord a New Song
section.sectionRationale: The fourth Hallelujah psalm calls God's people to sing a new song in the assembly of the godly, rejoicing in their Maker and King, and pictures praise itself as strength for the certain, final defeat of evil, an honor given to all His saints.
section.thesis: The LORD delights in His people and adorns the humble with salvation, and calls them to a joyful, wholehearted worship that is itself a weapon against evil, anticipating the new song of the redeemed before the Lamb, Revelation 5:9, and Christ's final victory over every rebellious power.
section.frameNote: Two movements: a call to joyful new praise in the assembly of the godly, verses 1-4; and praise as strength for the certain judgment God's people share in, verses 5-9.

units.label: Sing to the Lord a new song
units.note: Israel rejoices in her Maker and King, who delights in His people

verses.text: {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}! Sing to the LORD a {{shir-chadash|new song}}, His praise in the assembly of the {{chasidim|godly}}.
Let Israel rejoice in their Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King.
Let them praise His name with dancing, and make music to Him with tambourine and harp.
For the LORD takes pleasure in His people; He adorns the afflicted with salvation.

units.label: Let the high praises of God be in their mouths
units.note: praise as strength for God's people, and the certainty of His judgment

verses.text: Let the saints exult in glory; let them shout for joy upon their beds.
May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands,
to inflict vengeance on the nations and punishment on the peoples,
to bind their kings with chains and their nobles with shackles of iron,
to execute the judgment written against them. This honor is for all His saints. {{haleluyah|Hallelujah}}!

haleluyah.gloss: An imperative call, praise the LORD. It opens and closes each of the last five psalms of the Psalter, framing the whole collection's final movement as one continuous shout of praise.

shir-chadash.gloss: A new song, fresh praise for a fresh work of God. The same phrase anticipates the new song sung to the Lamb by the redeemed of every nation, Revelation 5:9.

chasidim.gloss: The godly ones, or saints, bound to God in covenant loving devotion, chesed. The same word describes the LORD's own people who exult in Him and carry out His judgment.

basic.context: This psalm calls the covenant community to sing a new song, joyful, embodied praise with dancing and instruments, because the LORD delights in His people and adorns the humble with salvation. It then pairs that praise with a picture of God's people executing His judgment on rebellious nations, an honor shared by all His saints.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a hymn of praise that moves into vivid, holy war imagery. Its historical setting envisions Israel as God's instrument of judgment on the nations; its abiding pattern is joyful, wholehearted praise and confident trust that God will finally set every wrong right.
basic.originalLanguages: The psalm opens and closes with haleluyah. It calls for a shir chadash, a new song, fresh praise for a fresh work of God. Those who sing are the chasidim, the godly ones bound to God in covenant loving devotion, who both praise and, in the psalm's imagery, carry out God's judgment.
basic.typology: The new song of verse 1 anticipates the new song sung to the Lamb by the redeemed of every tribe and nation, Revelation 5:9-10. The double-edged sword in the mouths and hands of God's people, verse 6, anticipates the word of God as a two-edged sword, Hebrews 4:12, and Christ Himself striking the nations with the sword from His mouth at His return, Revelation 19:15.
basic.christ: The praise and judgment this psalm holds together are fulfilled in Christ, who is Himself the Lamb who receives the new song of the redeemed, Revelation 5:9, and who alone executes final judgment on the nations with the sword of His mouth, Revelation 19:15, while entrusting His people now with the sword of the Spirit, the word of God, Ephesians 6:17.
basic.god: God is shown as the one who takes pleasure in His people and adorns the humble with salvation, who is worthy of ever fresh, joyful, embodied praise, and who is the final judge of every rebellious nation and king, a judgment His people share in and celebrate.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 5:9-10 pictures the redeemed of every nation singing a new song to the Lamb who ransomed them. Hebrews 4:12 calls the word of God living, active, and sharper than any double-edged sword. Revelation 19:15 shows Christ Himself striking down the nations with the sword from His mouth at His return.
basic.oneStory: God's people are called to ever fresh praise because the LORD delights in them and saves the humble, and that praise is bound up with confident hope in His final justice, fulfilled when Christ, the Lamb who receives the new song of the redeemed, returns to judge the nations and vindicate His saints forever.

context.literary:
Psalm 149 is a hymn with two halves that seem at first to belong to different poems. Verses 1 to 5 are a call to joyful worship, new song, dance, tambourine and harp, and the LORD's pleasure in His people. Verses 6 to 9 add a sword and chains and the execution of judgment. The way the two halves are joined deserves attention. Verse 6 does not start a new topic but continues the sentence of verse 5: 'let the saints exult... May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands.' The praise and the sword are held in the same breath, and the whole of the second half hangs on the single phrase 'in their mouths... in their hands.'

The first half is built on three summons about who is to rejoice: the assembly of the godly, Israel in their Maker, and the children of Zion in their King. Each is a name for the same community, and each is paired with a title of God, Maker and King. The reason in verse 4 is a plain statement of delight, and its object is the afflicted, so that the whole of the first half rests on the thought that God takes pleasure in people who have little to commend them. The joy of verse 5 reaches even the bed, 'upon their beds,' which is the place of private weariness or fear, so the praise is not confined to the temple.

The second half then runs through three infinitives that depend on the sword: to inflict vengeance, to bind kings, and to execute the judgment written. The progression is from the act, to the captives, to the authority behind it. The last words of verse 9, 'This honor is for all His saints,' return to the community of verse 1, and the psalm closes the circle with the same word for 'godly ones' that it opened with. The note of honour, a gift given to all, is the thing the final line wants remembered. The psalm is the fourth of the closing five, and its place matters: it sits just before the great finale of Psalm 150, as the Psalter moves from lament toward unbroken praise.
context.historical:
The psalm is easiest to understand against Israel's practice of praise in the face of battle. When Jehoshaphat faced an alliance of enemies, he appointed singers to go out before the army, singing, 'Give thanks to the LORD, for His loving devotion endures forever,' and the account says that the moment they began their shouts and praises, the LORD set ambushes against the enemy, 2 Chronicles 20:21-22. Worship and warfare were not in separate rooms. Israel's earliest great hymns follow a victory, and Miriam took a tambourine and led the women out with dancing after the sea, Exodus 15:20-21. David danced before the LORD with all his might, 2 Samuel 6:14. The instruments and movements of verse 3 belong to that world.

The vengeance on nations in verse 7 has a long Old Testament history behind it. It borrows from the language of the Song of Moses, where the LORD says that He will take vengeance on His adversaries and that the nations are to rejoice with His people, Deuteronomy 32:41-43. It also draws on the traditions of holy war in Deuteronomy 20, in which Israel was commanded to carry out judgment on specific nations, Deuteronomy 20:16-18. These were judgments with limits in time and place, directed at particular peoples, and the book of Joshua says plainly that the land was given and that the work was complete, Joshua 21:43-45. The psalm, however, speaks of 'the nations' and 'the peoples' and not of the old list of peoples, which indicates that its horizon is wider.

Later Jewish readers heard the sword in more than one way. In the days after the exile the builders of the wall worked with a tool in one hand and a weapon in the other, Nehemiah 4:17-18, and the community knew that the work of God was done under threat. The text itself says nothing about Israel taking the initiative. What it speaks of is the saints taking part in a judgment that the LORD has decided, and that is written, which is a different thing from a national campaign.
context.canonical:
Psalm 149 opens by borrowing the Psalter's own phrase for a fresh act of praise. The new song appears in Psalm 33:3, 40:3, 96:1, 98:1, and 144:9, and in Isaiah 42:10, where it is sung 'from the ends of the earth.' In every case a new song answers a new act of God, whether deliverance, forgiveness, or the coming of the LORD to judge the earth. Psalm 98:1 is nearest to this one, since it connects the new song to the LORD's victory.

The sword and the judgment are tied to the royal psalms. Psalm 2:8-9 offers the Son the nations as an inheritance and a rod of iron, Psalm 110:5-6 says that the Lord at the king's right hand will crush kings in the day of His wrath and judge the nations, and Psalm 149:8 talks of binding kings with chains. The prophets share the language: Isaiah 11:4 speaks of the rod of the mouth by which the Messiah strikes the earth and slays the wicked, and Joel 3:9-12 summons the nations to the valley of decision. Throughout, the decision about who wins belongs to the LORD, and where God's people appear, they appear as those who share in His judgment, not as those who start it.

The New Testament reads the sword in new ways. Hebrews 4:12 says that the word of God is sharper than any double-edged sword, Ephesians 6:17 names the sword of the Spirit as the word of God, and 2 Corinthians 10:3-5 says that the weapons of the believer's warfare are not worldly but have power to demolish strongholds and take every thought captive. Revelation 1:16 and 19:15 put the sword in the mouth of Christ, who strikes down the nations with it. At the same time, 1 Corinthians 6:2-3 says that the saints will judge the world and angels, Revelation 2:26-27 promises the one who overcomes authority over the nations, and Revelation 5:9-10 sets the new song in the mouths of the redeemed from every tribe and nation, who are made a kingdom and priests.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist wanted the people of God to find their voice and their courage together. The first half is meant to produce a community that sings and dances because it knows that its God is pleased with it. For a people who were afflicted and often small, that is the central good news. The LORD is not an examiner waiting for them to pass. He delights in them, and the word 'adorns' in verse 4 pictures Him dressing the humble in salvation as though it were a garment. Praise is the right reply to that, and the psalm asks for it to be loud, physical, and fresh.

The second half meant to tell them that they would not be at the mercy of the world's kings for ever. Israel's story was a story of oppression by empires with armies and chains, and a psalm that spoke of binding kings with iron and executing judgment was a promise that the powers that seemed permanent were not. It was meant to steady a people who might otherwise despair. The 'double-edged sword' ties this hope to the praise in their mouths, and the author does not separate the two. The line suggests that the people's confidence rests on worship: the ones who sing the high praises of God are the ones who can face the world's thrones without fear.

The psalm also wanted to show that the honour belongs to all. 'This honor is for all His saints' is a democratic note. The judgment is not reserved for priests, kings, or soldiers, and the poor and afflicted of verse 4 are the ones included. The hearers are told that they have a share in what God will do.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This is the psalm that most needs careful handling in this part of the Psalter, since a careless reading can license violence. The first half contains commands to praise that carry straight across, and the second half describes a role for the saints in a judgment of nations. Nothing in the psalm tells the people of God to take up swords on their own initiative. The language is jussive: 'Let the saints exult,' 'May the high praises of God be in their mouths.' These are wishes and expectations, and the judgment itself is described as 'written,' that is, already decided by God.

The New Testament is explicit about how believers now take part in this. Jesus told Peter to put his sword away, Matthew 26:52, and said before Pilate that His kingdom is not of this world and that His servants would otherwise fight, John 18:36. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a village, He rebuked them, Luke 9:54-56. Paul teaches that believers are not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God's wrath, Romans 12:19, and to overcome evil with good, Romans 12:21, while the state bears the sword as God's servant, Romans 13:4. The one who is told to love enemies, Matthew 5:44, is the one the psalm's judgments are entrusted to. The sword is the word of God, Ephesians 6:17, and the weapons of the church's warfare are not worldly, 2 Corinthians 10:4.

What carries forward is the joy, the freshness of the song, the confidence that wrong will be judged, and the sense of honour that all God's people share. What does not carry forward is the use of this psalm as a licence for religious violence. It has been misused for that purpose in the church's history, and a faithful reading must reject it.

debates.question: How should the sword and vengeance of verses 6 to 9 be understood?

views.label: As a literal judgment executed by God's people at the end
views.case: Some read the verses as looking to the final day, when Christ returns and the saints share in His judgment, 1 Corinthians 6:2-3 and Revelation 2:26-27. The vengeance is God's, and the saints share it as His agents. Revelation 19:15 puts the sword in Christ's mouth, and the armies of heaven follow Him, Revelation 19:14.

views.label: As spiritual warfare with the word of God
views.case: Others point to Hebrews 4:12, Ephesians 6:17, and 2 Corinthians 10:3-5, which treat the sword as the word of God and the warfare as the demolition of strongholds and arguments. The believer is called to carry the sword of the Spirit into a world of rival claims, and the binding of kings is the subduing of every power that exalts itself against God.

views.label: As Israel's historical role in God's judgments
views.case: A third reading takes the psalm as written for Israel at a time when it expected to share in the LORD's victories over its enemies, in the manner of Deuteronomy 32:41-43 and the holy war texts. The psalm would then be a hymn of that age, and the church receives it through Christ rather than as a call to repeat it.

debates.bearing: The three views agree on what is not allowed: private violence in God's name. The New Testament consistently places vengeance in God's hands and gives the church the word as its sword, so the best reading holds the psalm together with Romans 12:19-21 and with the return of Christ in Revelation 19.

debates.question: Who are the 'godly' or 'saints' of the psalm?

views.label: Israel, the covenant community
views.case: The psalm places the chasidim in parallel with 'Israel' and 'the children of Zion' in verse 2 and ends with 'Israel' in the same sense in Psalm 148:14. The godly are the people who are bound to God in covenant, and the psalm was sung by them.

views.label: The church as the people of Christ
views.case: The New Testament calls believers saints and treats the church as the people of God drawn from every nation, Ephesians 2:19 and Revelation 5:9-10. On this view the psalm's honour is shared by all who are in Christ.

debates.bearing: The two views are joined by the New Testament's teaching that Gentiles have been brought near and share in Israel's inheritance, Ephesians 2:12-13. The saints are the people of the LORD, and the psalm is read by the church as a family song.

study.originalLanguages:
The first phrase in verse 1 is shir chadash, 'a new song.' The adjective chadash means new in the sense of fresh or renewed, not necessarily unheard of, and it appears with 'song' at Psalm 33:3, 96:1, 98:1, and 144:9. The word is later used in Revelation 5:9 and 14:3, where the Greek kainos carries a similar idea of newness of quality and not only of time. The new song is a fresh answer to a fresh act of God.

The godly are the chasidim, in verses 1, 5, and 9, from the noun chesed, the loyal covenant love that is the LORD's own character in Psalm 147:11. A chasid is someone who shares in that loyalty, a person bound to God in love and faithfulness. The word appears in Psalm 30:4, where the chasidim are summoned to sing to the LORD, and in Psalm 132:9, where the priests are clothed with righteousness and the chasidim shout for joy. The English 'saints' and 'godly' both try to reach one word. The psalm uses it three times so that the single group that praises is the single group that will share the honour.

In verse 2 Israel is told to rejoice 'in their Maker' and 'in their King.' The verb is samach, to be glad, and its form here is a jussive, 'let them rejoice.' The preposition 'in' shows where their joy is found. Their delight is not in their own power but in who made them and who rules them.

Verse 4 says that the LORD 'adorns' the afflicted with salvation. The verb is pa'ar, to beautify or glorify, as in Isaiah 55:5 and 60:9, where God glorifies His people. The word translated 'afflicted' is anavim, the humble and poor, the same word that appears in Psalm 147:6. The word for 'salvation' is yeshuah, the word that stands behind the name of Jesus. The picture is of the poor being dressed in beauty with the LORD's own deliverance, much like the garment of praise that Isaiah 61:3 gives in place of a spirit of despair.

The 'high praises' of verse 6 are literally the exaltations, from the root rum, to be high, which also appears in Psalm 148:14 in the verb for raising up the horn. The line sets 'exaltations of God in their throat' beside a sword in their hand. The Hebrew for the weapon is a sword of mouths, an idiom for a double-edged blade, one that devours on both sides, and the same idiom for the sword is found in Judges 3:16. The mouths of the sword and the mouths of the saints are set in a play on words that English cannot keep.

In verse 7 the word for 'punishment' is tokhachot, from the root yakach, to reprove or rebuke, and so it means correction as well as penalty. In verse 9 the 'judgment written' is mishpat katuv. The text does not say where it is written, and the psalm is content to say that the verdict is already on record. The word for 'vengeance' is neqamah, which in Scripture belongs first to God, as Deuteronomy 32:35 and 32:41 show, and Paul quotes the former text in Romans 12:19.

typology.fulfillment: Each new song in the Psalter answers a new act of God, and the last of them is the song sung to the Lamb: 'Worthy are You to take the scroll and open its seals, because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9. The song is new because the act is new, the redemption of a people from every nation by the death of the Son. The correspondence is that a community praises its Redeemer in fresh words. The escalation is that the deliverance is no longer a victory over an army but over sin and death. The type is not exhausted, since the song of Revelation 14:3 is one that only the redeemed can learn, and the final song is sung when the work is complete.

typology.type: The LORD who adorns the afflicted with salvation, verse 4
typology.fulfillment: The humble are dressed with deliverance as if with a garment. Isaiah 61:3 gives them 'a garment of praise for a spirit of despair,' and Jesus reads that passage as His own work, Luke 4:18-21. The pattern is carried further in the parable of the father who clothes the returning son with the best robe, Luke 15:22, and in Paul's description of believers as clothed with Christ, Galatians 3:27. The beauty that the afflicted wear is borrowed, not their own. The type falls short only in that the full adornment is still to come, when the bride is given fine linen to wear, bright and pure, Revelation 19:7-8.

typology.type: The sword in the mouths and hands of the saints, verse 6
typology.fulfillment: The sword of the psalm is taken up as the word of God. Hebrews 4:12 says that the word is sharper than any double-edged sword, and Ephesians 6:17 calls the sword of the Spirit the word of God. The correspondence is real, but the New Testament changes the weapon. The saints do not fight with iron but with truth, and Paul says that the weapons of their warfare have divine power to demolish strongholds, 2 Corinthians 10:4-5. Christ Himself bears the sword in His mouth, Revelation 1:16 and 19:15. The type is therefore turned and not simply repeated, and it must never be taken as a pattern for literal violence.

typology.type: The binding of kings and the judgment written, verses 8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: The picture of kings in chains looks toward the day when every power is subdued. Psalm 110:5-6 says that the Lord will crush kings in the day of His wrath, and Paul says that Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet, 1 Corinthians 15:24-26. The saints share in that rule: they will judge the world, 1 Corinthians 6:2, and the one who overcomes is given authority over the nations, Revelation 2:26-27. The cross itself was the decisive stroke, for there Christ disarmed the powers and authorities and made a public spectacle of them, Colossians 2:15. The type is only partly fulfilled now, since the final judgment is still ahead, and Revelation 20:4 places the saints' reign at the end.

study.christ:
Psalm 149 leads to Christ first by the new song. When the Lamb takes the scroll, the elders and the living creatures sing, 'Worthy are You,' Revelation 5:9. The psalm's call to a fresh song is answered by the song of the redeemed, and the reason given is the cross: 'because You were slain, and by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation,' Revelation 5:9. The same redeemed are called 'a kingdom and priests to serve our God,' Revelation 5:10, which links to the psalm's picture of a people who are at once worshippers and sharers in rule. Christ is the one who makes the new song possible, and He is the one to whom it is sung.

It leads to Christ by the afflicted who are adorned. The psalm says that the LORD takes pleasure in His people and adorns the afflicted with salvation. The one who proclaims the favour of the LORD to the poor, and who reads in Nazareth that He will give a garment of praise for a spirit of despair, Isaiah 61:3 and Luke 4:18-21, is Jesus. Paul says that those who are in Christ have put on Christ, Galatians 3:27, and that God has clothed them with righteousness, Isaiah 61:10. What the humble wear is the salvation that Christ has won.

It leads to Christ by the sword and the judgment. The psalm gives to the saints a share in the execution of judgment, and the New Testament says that the final judgment belongs to Christ. John 5:22 says that the Father has entrusted all judgment to the Son. Revelation 19:11-16 shows Him as the rider called Faithful and True, with a sharp sword coming from His mouth to strike down the nations. The sword is in His mouth, not in His hand, which is a sign that it is the word of His command that does the work, as Isaiah 11:4 had said, 'He will strike the earth with the rod of His mouth.' The psalm's picture of kings in chains is carried out by the one who is 'KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS,' Revelation 19:16. The saints follow Him, in white linen, Revelation 19:14, and they have a share in what He does, but He is the one who does it.

The way Christ Himself wielded the sword also governs the way the psalm may be read. He did not take up a physical weapon. When Peter drew his sword, He said, 'Put your sword back in its place,' Matthew 26:52, and when He was reviled, 'He did not retaliate,' 1 Peter 2:23. The one who will execute judgment at the end first took judgment on Himself at the cross. That is why Paul can say, 'Do not avenge yourselves,' Romans 12:19: the vengeance is the Lord's, and He has shown that He is the one who bears the cost before He brings the verdict.

A caution is needed. Psalm 149 is not a prediction about Jesus in so many words, and the sword of verse 6 is not a hidden picture of a cross. The links rest on what the New Testament does with the imagery of the song, the sword, and the judgment of the kings. Christ is the one who sings with His people, Hebrews 2:12, and the one who judges, and the psalm's two halves meet in Him.
study.god:
The psalm shows first a God who delights in His people. 'The LORD takes pleasure in His people,' verse 4. The word for pleasure is the word used of favour and acceptance, and its subject is the God of the whole universe. The sentence is placed as the reason for all the singing and dancing that comes before it. The God of Psalm 149 is not a distant monarch who tolerates His subjects but one who is glad of them, and glad especially of the afflicted. That is the first doctrine of the psalm and it must be heard before the sword is mentioned.

He is a Maker and a King. In verse 2 Israel rejoices in both titles. As Maker, He has a claim on their existence, and as King He has a claim on their obedience. The two titles hold together the intimacy of origin and the authority of rule. A people who sing to their Maker are singing to the one who knows them from the inside.

He is a Saviour who clothes the humble. The verb 'adorns' says that salvation is a gift put on from outside, and not something people achieve. The poor are dressed in a beauty that is His. That is the pattern of grace through the whole Bible: God takes people who have nothing and gives them what they could not make.

He is a Judge. The second half of the psalm insists that God does not leave wrong unanswered. The nations that oppress, the kings who bind, and the nobles who hold others in iron are not outside His reach. The judgment is 'written,' which means it is not an improvisation or a sudden fit of anger but a verdict in keeping with His character and word. The same God who takes pleasure in the humble is the one who stands against the proud, and the two are not at odds, since one cannot be truly good and indifferent to evil.

He is a God who shares His work with His people. The psalm says that the honour belongs to all the saints, and the New Testament says that the saints will judge the world, 1 Corinthians 6:2, and reign with Christ, Revelation 20:4. God does not do things alone for the sake of it. He brings His people into His work, and He dignifies the poor with a share in His rule.

He is a God to be worshipped with the whole person. Dancing, tambourine, harp, shouting on the bed, and praise in the mouth are all used, so worship engages body, voice, and imagination. God is not only the object of the mind's assent but of the heart's joy.

The psalm also holds a tension that is part of its honesty. The same God is gentle with the afflicted and severe with the proud, and the psalm does not smooth the contrast. For worship, this means that praise is not sentimental. A believer can sing about a God who will set all wrongs right with a joy that has weight, because the delight in the first half rests on the justice in the second, and the confidence of the second half rests on the love of the first.

crossReferences.note: A new song for the LORD who has done wonders and whose right hand has gained the victory, who has revealed His righteousness to the nations. It shows what a new song answers in the Psalter, a fresh act of God, and its mention of the victory is the nearest parallel to the second half of Psalm 149.

After the sea, Miriam took a tambourine and all the women followed with tambourines and dancing, singing to the LORD who threw the horse and rider into the sea. It is the oldest example of the praise Psalm 149:3 asks for, and it shows that dancing and deliverance belonged together from the start.

Jehoshaphat sent singers before the army, and the moment they began praising, the LORD set ambushes against the enemy. It shows how praise and the LORD's judgment could be joined in Israel's life, with the singers going first and the LORD doing the fighting.

In the Song of Moses the LORD sharpens His sword and takes vengeance on His adversaries, and the nations are told to rejoice with His people. Its language lies behind the vengeance of Psalm 149:7, and it makes clear that vengeance is the LORD's, with the people sharing in the rejoicing.

The anointed one gives a crown of beauty for ashes and a garment of praise for a spirit of despair. It is the prophetic counterpart to the LORD adorning the afflicted with salvation in verse 4, and it ties both texts to the mission of Jesus.

The Lord at the king's right hand will crush kings in the day of His wrath and judge the nations. It stands behind the binding of kings in verse 8 and sets the judgment in the hands of the royal Son of David rather than of Israel's armies.

Scripture itself is described as a blade that pierces to the thoughts and intentions of the heart. The writer reapplies the sword image of Psalm 149:6 to the spoken and written word, which shows how the early church heard the psalm.

The sword of the Spirit is the word of God, part of the armour that Paul tells believers to wear against spiritual powers. It names the weapon of the saints in the present age, which is different from the iron the psalm's first hearers may have pictured.

The weapons of the believer's warfare are not worldly but have divine power to demolish strongholds and take every thought captive. It explains how the church can sing about the sword without picking one up, and it places the psalm's battle in the realm of arguments and allegiance.

Believers are told not to avenge themselves, because vengeance belongs to the Lord, and to overcome evil with good. It guards the reading of verse 7, since the New Testament quotes the very Old Testament passage that lies behind the psalm and places the act of vengeance in God's hands.

The redeemed of every tribe, tongue, people, and nation sing a new song to the Lamb who was slain. It is the final form of the new song of verse 1, and it shows the community of the psalm enlarged to every nation.

The rider called Faithful and True judges with righteousness, and a sharp sword comes from His mouth to strike down the nations. It shows the judgment of verses 7 to 9 executed by Christ, with the sword in His mouth and the saints following.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 149 draws on the oldest hymns of Israel. The first new song was sung on the far shore of the sea, when Miriam took up her tambourine and the women danced, Exodus 15:20-21. That song celebrated a deliverance in which the LORD overcame Pharaoh's army, and the Psalter's new songs echo it. Psalm 149 is the Psalter's fresh version, in which a community that has again been delivered picks up the instruments and the dance.

It also answers the question of what happens to the powers of this world. From the garden onward, human kings have used their authority against God's people, from Pharaoh to the empires that carried Israel away. The book of Psalms opens with the nations raging against the LORD and His anointed, Psalm 2:1-2, and the answer is that the One enthroned in heaven laughs and gives the Son the nations as His inheritance, Psalm 2:4-9. Psalm 149 reaches into that story and promises that kings will be bound and judgment will be executed, and that the people of God will not be forgotten under the weight of empires.

The story takes a turn in Christ. He enters the world as the afflicted one, but also as the King, and He sets the pattern for how the sword is to be used. He does not strike but is struck, and His victory over the powers comes at the cross, where He disarms the rulers and authorities, Colossians 2:15. Then He rises and sends the church into the world with the word of God as its sword, Ephesians 6:17, and with the instruction to love enemies. The song of the saints continues in a world that still has kings and chains, and the church sings it in the confidence that the verdict is already written.

At the end of the story the psalm's two halves are fulfilled together. The Lamb receives the new song from the redeemed of every nation, Revelation 5:9-10, and the rider on the white horse strikes the nations with the sword of His mouth, Revelation 19:15. The saints who had been under the altar crying for justice, Revelation 6:9-10, see it done, and the armies of heaven follow Him in white linen, Revelation 19:14. Those who were afflicted are adorned with salvation, and those who took pleasure in power are brought low.

The ending is not violence but a city. The kings of the earth who are not destroyed bring their glory into it, Revelation 21:24, and the throne of God and of the Lamb is at its centre, Revelation 22:3. The nations that were bound in verse 8 are healed by the leaves of the tree of life, Revelation 22:2, and the song that was new in Psalm 149 becomes the unending song of the redeemed, who 'will see His face,' Revelation 22:4. The sword has done its work and is laid down.

quiz.q: What are God's people called to sing, verse 1?

options.text: A new song, His praise in the assembly of the godly.
options.note: The psalm opens with a call to fresh, communal praise.

options.text: An old song, repeated exactly as before.
options.note: The psalm specifically calls for a new song, not mere repetition.

options.text: A song of complaint against their enemies.
options.note: The song is praise directed to God, not primarily complaint.

options.text: A private song, sung only in solitude.
options.note: The setting named is the assembly of the godly, a communal gathering.

quiz.q: According to verse 4, in whom does the LORD take pleasure?

options.text: In His people; He adorns the afflicted, or humble, with salvation.
options.note: God's delight rests on His own people, especially the humble whom He saves.

options.text: Only in kings and the powerful.
options.note: The verse specifically names the afflicted, or humble, not the powerful.

options.text: In no one; God takes pleasure in nothing.
options.note: The verse states the opposite, that the LORD takes pleasure in His people.

options.text: Only in angels, not in human beings.
options.note: The verse is explicitly about God's own human people, not angels.

quiz.q: What two things are described together in verse 6?

options.text: The high praises of God in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands.
options.note: Worship and readiness for God's judgment are pictured side by side.

options.text: A crown and a scepter.
options.note: The verse names praise and a sword, not royal regalia.

options.text: Silence and mourning.
options.note: The verse describes vocal praise, not silence.

options.text: A harp and a lyre only.
options.note: Instruments appear earlier, in verse 3; verse 6 pairs praise with a sword image.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament reframe the sword imagery of this psalm?

options.text: As the word of God, a double-edged sword, Hebrews 4:12, and the sword of the Spirit, Ephesians 6:17, with final judgment executed by Christ Himself, Revelation 19:15.
options.note: The New Testament transforms literal warfare imagery into the power of God's word and Christ's own final judgment.

options.text: By commanding believers to take up literal weapons against unbelievers.
options.note: The New Testament explicitly teaches the opposite, that Christ's kingdom does not advance by earthly force, John 18:36.

options.text: By removing all mention of judgment from Christian teaching.
options.note: Judgment remains a real New Testament theme, though entrusted finally to Christ rather than to human armies.

options.text: By applying it only to Israel's ancient enemies, with no ongoing relevance.
options.note: The New Testament reapplies the imagery meaningfully to the word of God and Christ's return, not merely as a closed historical footnote.

quiz.q: What connects this psalm's new song to Revelation?

options.text: Revelation 5:9-10 pictures the redeemed of every nation singing a new song to the Lamb who ransomed them.
options.note: This is a direct thematic and verbal echo of Psalm 149:1's call for a new song.

options.text: Revelation forbids any new songs of praise.
options.note: Revelation celebrates, rather than forbids, the new song of the redeemed.

options.text: The connection is only to Revelation's judgment scenes, not its songs.
options.note: The clearest connection is specifically to Revelation's scenes of song, Revelation 5:9-10.

options.text: The connection exists but is considered minor by most interpreters.
options.note: The new song motif is a widely recognized, significant link between this psalm and Revelation.

questions: God's people are called to sing a new song, verse 1. What fresh reason for praise has God given you recently that deserves fresh words, not just old routines?
The LORD adorns the afflicted, or humble, with salvation, verse 4, and delights in His humble people. Where do you need to receive that truth about yourself rather than striving to earn His favor?
This psalm pairs high praises with a readiness for spiritual battle, verse 6. What would it look like to let praise fuel your resistance to a specific temptation or struggle this week?
The final judgment pictured here is now entrusted to Christ and proclaimed through His word. How does trusting God's ultimate justice free you from taking vengeance into your own hands?
This honor is for all His saints, verse 9. How does knowing you share in Christ's ultimate victory shape your everyday courage?

translationNotes.note: Afflicted, also rendered humble, renders a Hebrew word describing those who are lowly or bowed down, whom the LORD adorns with salvation.
Double-edged sword renders a Hebrew phrase for a sword with two mouths, or edges, the same image Hebrews 4:12 applies to the word of God.
